senses.gloss: Coming from outside a person or thing, not part of its basic nature.
examples: Grades and money are *extrinsic* rewards; curiosity is an intrinsic one.
The value of a dollar bill is *extrinsic* — the paper itself is worth almost nothing.
Researchers looked at both genetic and *extrinsic* factors.

senses.gloss: Outgoing and full of energy around other people; enjoying company.
examples: She's very *extroverted* and loves meeting new people.
My *extroverted* brother talks to everyone on the bus.
I'm *more extroverted* at work than I am at home.

senses.gloss: Full of energy, excitement and happiness.
examples: The *exuberant* fans poured onto the field.
The kids were *exuberant* on the last day of school.
Her *exuberant* laugh filled the room.

senses.gloss: Growing thickly and strongly, or bright and full of life in style.
examples: The garden was a mass of *exuberant* green.
The painting uses *exuberant* reds and yellows.

senses.gloss: Attractive or unusual enough to make people notice it.
examples: The store needs an *eye-catching* sign.
Her red coat was very *eye-catching*.
Which of these two designs is *more eye-catching*?

senses.gloss: So large, surprising or striking that it makes you stare — informal.
examples: The house sold for an *eye-popping* $4 million.
The special effects were *eye-popping*.
The team put up *eye-popping* numbers this season.

senses.gloss: Famous and talked about a lot, often in stories that may not be completely true.
examples: We finally drove the *fabled* Route 66.
The team's *fabled* 1927 lineup is still talked about today.
The city is *fabled* for its jazz clubs.

senses.gloss: Invented in order to deceive people; not true.
examples: The reporter was fired for publishing *fabricated* quotes.
His lawyers say the evidence was *fabricated*.
She told a completely *fabricated* story about her past.

senses.gloss: Extremely good; wonderful — informal.
examples: You look *fabulous* in that dress!
We had a *fabulous* time in New Orleans.
The view from the top was *fabulous*.

senses.gloss: Unusually great in amount or size.
examples: He made a *fabulous* fortune in oil.
The family lived in *fabulous* wealth.

senses.gloss: Helping someone avoid looking foolish or losing other people's respect.
examples: The two sides agreed on a *face-saving* compromise.
Resigning was a *face-saving* move for the senator.
They needed a *face-saving* way to end the strike.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *a face-to-face meeting*
contrast: After a verb it is often the adverb, usually written open: *We finally met face to face*.

senses.gloss: With the people physically together in the same place, not by phone or online.
examples: I'd rather have a *face-to-face* conversation about this.
Classes will be *face-to-face* again this fall.
Nothing replaces *face-to-face* contact with customers.

senses.gloss: Having no individual character; impersonal and unknown.
examples: I'm tired of dealing with *faceless* bureaucrats.
The *faceless* office towers all looked the same.
Big corporations can seem *faceless* and cold.

senses.gloss: Joking about something serious, or not meaning what you say to be taken seriously.
examples: Don't be *facetious* — this is important.
I was being *facetious* when I said I'd quit.
He made a *facetious* comment about the funeral.

contrast: *A facial* is also a noun: a beauty treatment for the face.

senses.gloss: Of or on the face.
examples: His *facial* expression didn't change.
The phone uses *facial* recognition to unlock.
He has a lot of *facial* hair.

contrast: Usually not a compliment: it does not simply mean 'easy' (лёгкий). *A facile answer* is too simple to be taken seriously.

senses.gloss: Too simple; not showing careful thought.
examples: That's a *facile* explanation for a complicated problem.
Critics called the book's conclusions *facile*.
There are no *facile* solutions to poverty.

senses.gloss: Done with little effort; smooth and fluent, sometimes too much so.
examples: The Yankees won a *facile* victory.
He's a *facile* writer who can turn out a column in an hour.

senses.gloss: Done to find out the facts about a situation.
examples: The senator went on a *fact-finding* trip to the border.
A *fact-finding* committee will look into the accident.
The first meeting is a *fact-finding* session.

senses.gloss: Made by machines in a factory, not by hand or at home.
examples: *Factory-made* furniture is cheaper but doesn't last as long.
Are these cookies homemade or *factory-made*?
Almost all the bread in the store is *factory-made*.

contrast: Russian *фактический* often means *actual* or *real*: *фактическая стоимость* is *the actual cost*. English *factual* means only 'based on facts' or 'about facts': *a factual report*, *a factual error*.

senses.gloss: Based on facts or containing facts, not opinions.
examples: The report contains several *factual* errors.
Please keep your answers short and *factual*.
The second article was *more factual* and less emotional.

senses.gloss: Having lost its color or brightness.
examples: He wore an old pair of *faded* jeans.
The sign on the barn was *faded* and hard to read.
The photo was *more faded* than I remembered.

senses.gloss: No longer strong, famous or clear.
examples: She's a *faded* movie star living in Palm Springs.
I have only *faded* memories of that house.

position: after the noun — after a number of degrees: *72 degrees Fahrenheit*; also before a noun: *the Fahrenheit scale*
contrast: Americans use *Fahrenheit* for weather, cooking and body temperature: 32°F is freezing and 98.6°F is normal body temperature. Always with a capital F.

senses.gloss: Measured on the temperature scale on which water freezes at 32 degrees and boils at 212.
examples: It was 95 degrees *Fahrenheit* in Phoenix today.
Bake at 350 degrees *Fahrenheit* for 25 minutes.
Most Americans only know the *Fahrenheit* scale.

senses.gloss: Designed to stay safe if something goes wrong; certain to work.
examples: The elevator has a *fail-safe* braking system.
There's no *fail-safe* way to pick stocks.
The system is supposed to be *fail-safe*.

position: attributive only — *failing health*; after *be* it is usually the verb: *His health is failing*
contrast: *A failing* is also a noun, meaning a weakness: *We all have our failings*.

senses.gloss: Becoming weaker or worse.
examples: She moved in with her daughter because of *failing* health.
In the *failing* light we couldn't see the trail.
Grandpa's *failing* eyesight means he can't drive anymore.

senses.gloss: Not successful; losing money, customers or support.
examples: He took over a *failing* restaurant and turned it around.
The state stepped in to fix *failing* schools.

senses.gloss: Of a grade or score: too low to pass.
examples: He got a *failing* grade in chemistry.
Anything below 60 counts as a *failing* score.

ru: слабый, едва заметный; близкий к обмороку
position: both — in the 'about to pass out' sense only after a verb: *I feel faint*
contrast: *I don't have the faintest idea* means 'I have no idea at all'. *Faint* is also a verb, 'to lose consciousness' (*She fainted*). *Feint* (a fake move) sounds the same.

senses.gloss: Hard to see, hear or smell; not strong.
examples: There was a *faint* smell of smoke in the hall.
The music grew *fainter* as we walked away.
I could see a *faint* light in the distance.

senses.gloss: Very small; slight.
examples: There's still a *faint* hope that they'll find survivors.
I don't have the *faintest* idea where he went.
She gave a *faint* smile.

senses.gloss: Feeling weak and dizzy, as if you are about to lose consciousness.
examples: I felt *faint* from the heat.
She was *faint* with hunger after the long hike.

contrast: Most often met in *not for the fainthearted* (not for people who scare easily), where *the fainthearted* is a noun.

senses.gloss: Lacking courage; easily frightened or discouraged.
examples: *Fainthearted* investors sold everything when prices fell.
Congress has been too *fainthearted* to raise taxes.
Don't be so *fainthearted* — just ask her out.

position: both — in the 'fairly large' sense only before a noun: *a fair number*
takes: *to* + person: *It isn't fair to her*; *to*-infinitive in *it's fair to say*
contrast: Russian *светлый* about hair and skin is *fair* in a slightly formal style; everyday American English more often says *blond* hair and *light* or *pale* skin. *A fair* is a noun (*the county fair*), and in *play fair* the word is an adverb.

senses.gloss: Treating people equally and according to the rules; just.
examples: It's not *fair* that she gets more money for the same job.
The judge was strict but *fair*.
Everyone deserves a *fair* trial.

senses.gloss: Reasonable and acceptable in the circumstances.
examples: We got a *fair* price for the car.
That's a *fair* question.
It's *fair* to say the plan didn't work.

senses.gloss: Fairly large in amount, number or distance.
examples: It's a *fair* distance from here to the lake.
A *fair* number of people left early.

senses.gloss: Neither very good nor very bad; average.
examples: His condition is only *fair* after the surgery.
The car is in *fair* shape for its age.

senses.gloss: Of hair or skin: light in color.
examples: People with *fair* skin burn easily.
She has *fairer* hair than her sister.
The baby had *fair* curls.

senses.gloss: Of weather: pleasant and dry, without rain.
examples: The forecast is *fair* and sunny for the weekend.
We sailed out under *fair* skies.

position: both — in the 'favorite' sense only before a noun: *the boss's fair-haired boy*

senses.gloss: Having light-colored hair.
examples: A *fair-haired* girl answered the door.
Both boys are *fair-haired* like their dad.

senses.gloss: Favored by someone in power — in *fair-haired boy*, informal American.
examples: He's the boss's *fair-haired* boy and gets every promotion.
For a few years she was the network's *fair-haired* girl.

senses.gloss: Judging people and situations fairly, without prejudice.
examples: We need a *fair-minded* person to settle this.
Most *fair-minded* voters would agree.
He's *more fair-minded* than most of his colleagues.

takes: *to* + person, belief or original: *faithful to his wife*, *faithful to the book*
contrast: About a husband, wife or partner, *faithful* means not having sex with anyone else, and *unfaithful* means cheating.

senses.gloss: Loyal; staying with a person, belief or group.
examples: Max was a *faithful* dog who followed her everywhere.
She's been a *faithful* customer for twenty years.
He stayed *faithful* to his wife for fifty years.

senses.gloss: Accurate; true to the original.
examples: The movie is *faithful* to the novel.
It's the *most faithful* translation I've read.

comparison: not gradable — but about insincere people *so fake* and *more fake* are common in speech
contrast: *Fake* vs *false*: *fake* is for copies made to fool people (*fake money*, *a fake ID*); *false* is for things that are not true (*a false statement*) and a few replacements (*false teeth*). *Fake* is also a verb (*He faked an injury*) and a noun (*The painting is a fake*).

senses.gloss: Made to look like something real, to trick people or to cost less.
examples: The police arrested him for using a *fake* ID.
Is that fur real or *fake*?
The site is full of *fake* reviews.

senses.gloss: Pretended; not sincere.
examples: She gave me a big *fake* smile.
I can't stand him — he's so *fake*.
His Southern accent sounds *fake*.

senses.gloss: Based on a false idea or bad reasoning — formal.
examples: The argument is *fallacious* because it assumes what it tries to prove.
The ad makes several *fallacious* claims.
Critics called the report's reasoning *fallacious*.

contrast: *The fallen* is also a noun: soldiers killed in war.

senses.gloss: Lying on the ground after falling.
examples: The yard was covered in *fallen* leaves.
A *fallen* tree blocked the road.

senses.gloss: Killed in a war.
examples: Memorial Day honors *fallen* soldiers.
The town built a monument to its *fallen* heroes.

senses.gloss: Having lost power, status or a good moral reputation.
examples: The movie is about a *fallen* star trying to make a comeback.
The *fallen* dictator fled the country.

position: attributive only — after *be* it is the verb: *Prices are falling*

senses.gloss: Coming down toward the ground.
examples: Watch out for *falling* rocks.
He was hit by a *falling* branch.
A *falling* star streaked across the sky.

senses.gloss: Going down in amount or level.
examples: *Falling* prices are good news for shoppers.
The company is struggling with *falling* sales.

senses.gloss: Able to make mistakes or be wrong.
examples: Doctors are human and *fallible* like everyone else.
Memory is *fallible*, so write it down.
Eyewitness testimony is *more fallible* than most juries think.

position: both — often in *lie fallow* and *leave fallow*

senses.gloss: Of farmland: left without crops for a season so the soil can recover.
examples: The farmer leaves one field *fallow* every year.
Weeds grew over the *fallow* land.

senses.gloss: Of a period of time: when little is done or produced.
examples: After his first hit, he went through a long *fallow* period.
The *fallow* years between albums were hard for the band.

position: both — in the 'artificial' sense only before a noun: *false teeth*
contrast: *False* vs *fake*: *a false statement* is not true; *a fake Rolex* is a copy made to fool you. Russian *фальшивые деньги* are *counterfeit* or *fake money*, not *false money*.

senses.gloss: Not true or correct.
examples: The rumor turned out to be *false*.
True or *false*: the sun is a star.
He gave the police a *false* name.

senses.gloss: Based on a mistake; wrong.
examples: It was a *false* alarm — there was no fire.
Don't give her *false* hope.
I had a *false* impression of him.

senses.gloss: Not natural; artificial.
examples: My grandfather has *false* teeth.
She wore *false* eyelashes to the party.

senses.gloss: Not sincere; pretended.
examples: Spare me the *false* modesty.
Her cheerfulness sounded *false*.

position: attributive only — after *be* it is usually the verb: *The economy is faltering*

senses.gloss: Weak or unsteady and likely to stop or fail.
examples: The tax cuts were meant to boost the *faltering* economy.
The coach tried to save his *faltering* career.
She took a few *faltering* steps.

senses.gloss: Of speech: hesitant and full of pauses.
examples: He answered in *faltering* English.
In a *faltering* voice, she thanked the crowd.

senses.gloss: Famous — used mostly in writing.
examples: We ate at the *famed* diner on Main Street.
The town is *famed* for its maple syrup.
She studied under the *famed* architect Frank Gehry.

contrast: Formal and medical; in everyday speech use *family* before a noun: *family ties*, *family history*. Don't confuse it with *familiar* (знакомый).

senses.gloss: Relating to a family, or passed down through families.
examples: The disease has a strong *familial* link.
She felt a strong sense of *familial* duty.
The study looked at *familial* patterns of heart disease.

position: both — usually after a verb: *I'm famished*
comparison: not gradable — an extreme adjective: *absolutely famished*

senses.gloss: Extremely hungry — informal.
examples: I'm *famished* — let's get something to eat.
The kids came home from practice *famished*.
A couple of *famished* hikers wandered into the diner.

senses.gloss: Extremely enthusiastic about something, often too much.
examples: He's *fanatical* about keeping his car clean.
The band has a *fanatical* following.
She became even *more fanatical* about fitness after college.

senses.gloss: Based on imagination rather than facts; not realistic.
examples: The idea that we'll finish by Friday is a little *fanciful*.
His story sounded *fanciful*, but it was true.

senses.gloss: Decorated in an unusual, imaginative way.
examples: The gates were covered in *fanciful* ironwork.
The book has *fanciful* drawings of dragons and castles.

contrast: Only the adjective is common in American English; *I fancy you* (I like you) and *Fancy a drink?* are British. *Nothing fancy* means simple and ordinary.

senses.gloss: Expensive and stylish, for rich or important people.
examples: They took us to a *fancy* restaurant downtown.
We stayed at the *fanciest* hotel in town.
Don't get too dressed up — it's not a *fancy* party.

senses.gloss: Decorated; not plain.
examples: The cake had *fancy* decorations on top.
I just want a plain T-shirt, nothing *fancy*.

senses.gloss: Complicated, clever or technically advanced.
examples: You don't need a *fancy* camera to take good photos.
The coach doesn't like *fancy* moves — just pass the ball.
He uses a lot of *fancy* words to sound smart.

contrast: In everyday speech *fantastic* usually means 'wonderful'; *fantastical* keeps the older meaning 'strange and imaginary'.

senses.gloss: Strange and imaginary, like something from a dream or a fairy tale.
examples: The film is set in a *fantastical* world of talking animals.
Her paintings are full of *fantastical* creatures.
The costumes were even *more fantastical* than the sets.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *far-left groups*
contrast: *The far left*, with no hyphen, is the noun: the people with the most extreme left-wing views.

senses.gloss: Holding very extreme left-wing political views.
examples: The *far-left* candidate won only 3 percent of the vote.
Some voters see his views as *far-left*.
The protest was organized by several *far-left* groups.

senses.gloss: Very far away.
examples: She's traveled to *far-flung* places like Mongolia and Chile.
The company has offices in *far-flung* corners of the world.

senses.gloss: Spread out over a large area.
examples: My family is so *far-flung* that we rarely all meet.
The empire was huge and *far-flung*.

position: attributive only — after a verb use *far off* or *far away*: *The day is not far off*

senses.gloss: Distant in space or time.
examples: The story takes place in a *far-off* land.
We could hear *far-off* thunder.
Retirement still seems like a *far-off* dream.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *far-right parties*
contrast: *The far right*, with no hyphen, is the noun: the people with the most extreme right-wing views.

senses.gloss: Holding very extreme right-wing political views.
examples: The *far-right* party gained seats in parliament.
Critics called the website *far-right*.
Police are watching several *far-right* groups.

position: attributive only — after a verb use two words: *The town is far away*

senses.gloss: Distant.
examples: She dreamed of *faraway* places.
We could see the lights of a *faraway* town.

senses.gloss: Of a look or voice: dreamy, as if thinking about something else.
examples: He had a *faraway* look in his eyes.
She answered in a *faraway* voice.

senses.gloss: So badly organized or silly that it is ridiculous.
examples: The trial was a *farcical* waste of time.
The meeting became *farcical* when nobody could find the agenda.
Each excuse was *more farcical* than the last.

senses.gloss: Very unlikely to be true or to happen.
examples: His excuse sounded pretty *farfetched*.
The plot of the movie is *farfetched* but fun.
It's not as *farfetched* as it sounds.

contrast: In American English the eye words are *farsighted* (дальнозоркий) and *nearsighted* (близорукий); British English says *long-sighted* and *short-sighted*.

senses.gloss: Able to see things far away clearly, but not things close to you.
examples: I'm *farsighted*, so I need glasses to read.
Many people become *farsighted* after forty.

senses.gloss: Thinking carefully about the future and planning for it.
examples: Buying land there in the 1970s was a *farsighted* decision.
The city's *farsighted* leaders built the subway early.

comparison: more/most — mostly in the insulting sense: *more fascist*
contrast: *Fascist* is the general word for this kind of politics; *Nazi* is specific to Hitler's Germany. *A fascist* is also a noun.

senses.gloss: Relating to fascism: rule by a dictator, with extreme nationalism and no opposition allowed.
examples: Mussolini led Italy's *fascist* government.
The group was banned for spreading *fascist* ideas.

senses.gloss: Very controlling and intolerant — used as an insult.
examples: My old boss was totally *fascist* about the dress code.
Protesters called the new law *fascist*.

senses.gloss: Popular at a particular time, or used by people who follow the latest style.
examples: She always wears *fashionable* clothes.
They live in a *fashionable* neighborhood in Brooklyn.
Small weddings have become *more fashionable* lately.

position: both — in the 'clock' sense only after a verb: *My watch is fast*; in *fast friends* only before a noun
contrast: *Fast* is also the adverb: *drive fast*, never *fastly*. *Fast* is mostly about speed (*a fast car*); *quick* is about taking a short time (*a quick question*), though they often overlap. In *fast asleep* it means 'firmly', and the verb *to fast* means to go without food.

senses.gloss: Moving or able to move at high speed.
examples: He drives a really *fast* car.
She's the *fastest* runner on the team.
The *fast* lane is on the left.

senses.gloss: Doing something or happening in a short time.
examples: He's a *fast* learner.
The internet here is much *faster* than at home.
We need a *fast* decision.

senses.gloss: Of a clock or watch: showing a time later than the real time.
examples: My watch is five minutes *fast*.
The clock in the car is *fast*, so don't panic.

senses.gloss: Firm and lasting — in *fast friends*, and of dye that does not wash out.
examples: The two girls became *fast* friends at camp.
Wash it in cold water — the dye isn't *fast*.

position: predicative only — *The baby is fast asleep*, not *a fast asleep baby*
contrast: Here *fast* does not mean 'quick': *fast asleep* means sleeping deeply, not falling asleep quickly.

senses.gloss: Sleeping deeply.
examples: By nine o'clock the kids were *fast asleep*.
I found him *fast asleep* on the couch.
She was *fast asleep* before the movie ended.

senses.gloss: Growing or getting bigger quickly.
examples: Austin is one of the *fastest-growing* cities in the country.
Bamboo is a *fast-growing* plant.
The company is small but *fast-growing*.

senses.gloss: Happening or moving quickly, with a lot going on.
examples: She works in a *fast-paced* newsroom.
The movie is *fast-paced* and full of action.
Life in New York is *faster-paced* than in Ohio.

senses.gloss: Very careful about details, cleanliness or order, sometimes too careful.
examples: He's *fastidious* about keeping his desk clean.
The restaurant is run by a *fastidious* chef.
When it comes to grammar, she's *more fastidious* than anyone I know.

contrast: *Fat-free* means with no fat at all; *low-fat* means with a little. *Fat-free* food can still be high in sugar and calories.

senses.gloss: Containing no fat.
examples: I'll have a *fat-free* latte, please.
This yogurt is *fat-free* but full of sugar.
The store only sells *fat-free* milk.

takes: *to* + person or thing: *fatal to her campaign*
contrast: Russian *фатальный* often means 'fateful' or 'inevitable'; English *fatal* means 'causing death' or 'causing ruin'. *A fatal accident* is one in which someone died. For 'deciding the future', use *fateful*.

senses.gloss: Causing death.
examples: There was a *fatal* accident on the highway last night.
The disease is almost always *fatal*.
He suffered a *fatal* heart attack.

senses.gloss: Causing failure or very bad results.
examples: Trusting him was a *fatal* mistake.
The plan has one *fatal* flaw.
The scandal proved *fatal* to her campaign.

senses.gloss: Believing that events are decided by fate and cannot be changed.
examples: He's *fatalistic* about his health — he says what will be will be.
She has a very *fatalistic* view of politics.
Older voters were *more fatalistic* about the economy.

position: both — usually after a verb with a *to*-infinitive: *fated to fail*

senses.gloss: Certain to happen or to do something, as if fate has decided it.
examples: Their marriage seemed *fated* to fail from the start.
Do you think we were *fated* to meet?
The novel tells the story of two *fated* lovers.

position: both — usually before a noun: *that fateful day*
contrast: *Fateful* means having a very important, often bad, effect on the future; *fatal* means causing death or ruin. *A fateful decision* changed everything; *a fatal decision* led to disaster.

senses.gloss: Having an important, often bad, effect on the future.
examples: On that *fateful* morning, she decided to take the train.
It was a *fateful* decision that changed his life.
The *fateful* meeting took place in 1962.

senses.gloss: Without a father, because he has died or is not part of the child's life.
senses.ru: оставшийся без отца, растущий без отца
examples: She grew up *fatherless* after her dad died in the war.
The charity helps *fatherless* children.
Millions of kids are growing up *fatherless*.

contrast: *Fatigued* is formal or medical; in conversation say *tired* or *exhausted*.

senses.gloss: Very tired — formal.
examples: Patients may feel *fatigued* for several weeks.
The *fatigued* soldiers slept wherever they could.
I felt *more fatigued* after the second dose.

senses.gloss: Likely to make you gain weight.
examples: I love fries, but they're so *fattening*.
Try to avoid *fattening* snacks late at night.
Is beer *more fattening* than wine?

contrast: *Fatty* describes food and body tissue; a person is *fat* or, more politely, *overweight*. As a noun, *fatty* is a rude name for a fat person.

senses.gloss: Containing a lot of fat.
examples: Cut down on *fatty* foods like burgers and fries.
This cut of meat is *fattier* than chicken breast.
The soup was too *fatty* for me.

senses.gloss: Made of fat or relating to fat in the body — in medicine and science.
examples: Doctors found *fatty* deposits in his arteries.
Omega-3 is a type of *fatty* acid.

senses.gloss: Without any mistakes; perfect.
examples: Her English is *faultless*.
The pianist gave a *faultless* performance.
His driving record is *faultless*.

senses.gloss: Not working correctly, or not made correctly.
examples: The fire was caused by *faulty* wiring.
The company recalled thousands of *faulty* airbags.
If the charger is *faulty*, the store will replace it.

senses.gloss: Of reasoning or information: containing mistakes.
examples: The study was based on *faulty* data.
That's *faulty* logic.

form: -ian from *Faust*, the man in the legend who sold his soul to the devil
contrast: Almost always in *a Faustian bargain* or *a Faustian deal*: giving up your values or your future for power, money or success now. Always with a capital F.

senses.gloss: Giving up something morally important in exchange for power, money or success.
examples: He made a *Faustian* bargain with the donors who paid for his campaign.
Taking the money was a *Faustian* deal she later regretted.
The novel explores the *Faustian* temptations of fame.

contrast: Pronounced FOH: the x is silent, as in French. In stores *faux* is the polite word, so *faux leather* sounds better than *fake leather*.

senses.gloss: Made to look like a real material; artificial.
examples: She bought a *faux* fur coat.
The chairs are covered in *faux* leather.
The kitchen has *faux* marble countertops.

senses.gloss: Pretended; not sincere — often humorous.
examples: He answered with *faux* innocence.
She let out a gasp of *faux* surprise.

takes: *to* or *toward* + an idea or person (approving of it); *for* + what it helps

senses.gloss: Showing approval; positive.
examples: The movie got *favorable* reviews.
Most voters have a *favorable* opinion of her.
The board was *favorable* to the idea.

senses.gloss: Good for someone or something; likely to help success.
examples: Conditions are *favorable* for the launch.
We got a loan on *favorable* terms.
Interest rates are *more favorable* now than last year.

takes: *to*-infinitive in the 'expected to win' sense: *favored to win*

senses.gloss: Preferred; liked more than others.
examples: Bikes are the *favored* way to get around campus.
It's a *favored* vacation spot for wealthy New Yorkers.
This was the *most favored* option in the survey.

senses.gloss: Expected to win.
examples: The Lakers are heavily *favored* to win tonight.
She's the *favored* candidate in the race.

position: attributive only — *my favorite song*; after a verb it is the noun: *This one is my favorite*
comparison: not gradable — *most favorite* is heard but avoided in careful English
contrast: *Favorite* already means 'liked most', so *my most favorite* is redundant. In sports, *the favorite* (a noun) is the team or player expected to win.

senses.gloss: Liked more than all others of the same kind.
examples: What's your *favorite* movie?
Pizza is my *favorite* food.
We went back to our *favorite* restaurant for our anniversary.

form: -ing from the verb *fawn* (*over* someone), to flatter
contrast: The verb *fawn* has nothing to do with *a fawn*, a baby deer (оленёнок).

senses.gloss: Praising someone too much in order to win their approval.
examples: The singer was surrounded by *fawning* fans.
The article was a *fawning* profile of the CEO.
Critics said the interview was far too *fawning*.

contrast: Almost always with a negative: *not fazed*, *didn't seem fazed*. It sounds the same as *phased* (*phased out*), which is a different word.

senses.gloss: Worried, confused or upset by something — usually with *not*.
examples: She wasn't *fazed* by the tough questions.
The pilot didn't seem *fazed* at all.
The kids weren't *fazed* by the long drive.

takes: *of* + noun or *-ing*; *that*-clause; *for* + the person you are worried about
contrast: *Fearful* is more formal than *afraid* or *scared* and describes the person who feels fear; *fearsome* describes what causes it.

senses.gloss: Afraid, or worried that something bad will happen.
examples: Many residents are *fearful* of another flood.
The dog gave a *fearful* look and ran away.
Parents are *more fearful* for their kids' safety than they used to be.

senses.gloss: Not afraid of anything.
examples: She's a *fearless* reporter who will ask anyone anything.
Little kids can be totally *fearless* around water.
He grew *more fearless* with every climb.

senses.gloss: Frightening, or so powerful that people are afraid of it.
examples: The team has a *fearsome* defense.
The grizzly bear is a *fearsome* animal.
The storm looked *fearsome* on the radar.

senses.gloss: Possible to do and likely to work.
examples: Is it *feasible* to finish the project by June?
We need a *feasible* plan, not a dream.
Solar power is becoming *more feasible* every year.

senses.gloss: Having or covered with feathers.
examples: Some dinosaurs were *feathered*.
She wore a *feathered* hat to the Kentucky Derby.
Our *feathered* friends need extra food in winter.

senses.gloss: Of hair: cut in soft layers that are brushed back from the face.
examples: *Feathered* hair was hugely popular in the 1970s.
He still has the *feathered* haircut he had in high school.

senses.gloss: Soft, light or thin, like a feather.
examples: Dill has *feathery* green leaves.
*Feathery* clouds drifted across the sky.
The snow was light and *feathery*.

senses.gloss: Given special attention as an important part of an event, show or page.
examples: Tonight's *featured* speaker is the governor.
Check out the *featured* products on our home page.
The album's *featured* artists include several big names.

senses.gloss: Relating to feces, the solid waste from the body — medical and technical.
examples: The beach was closed because of *fecal* bacteria in the water.
The doctor ordered a *fecal* test.
*Fecal* matter can contaminate drinking water.

senses.gloss: Lacking the ability, effort or will to do anything useful; irresponsible.
examples: Her *feckless* brother keeps asking to borrow money.
Critics called the city council *feckless*.
The leadership has never looked *more feckless*.

ru: сытый по горло, доведённый до предела
position: predicative only — *I'm fed up*, not *a fed up person*
contrast: Americans say *fed up with*; *fed up of* is heard in British speech but is avoided in careful English.

senses.gloss: Annoyed and tired of something that has gone on too long.
senses.ru: сытый по горло, доведённый до предела
examples: I'm *fed up* with this traffic.
Voters are *fed up* with both parties.
She finally got *fed up* and quit.

contrast: In the US, *federal* means the national government in Washington, as opposed to the state governments: *federal taxes* vs *state taxes*, *a federal crime*. Russian *федеративное государство* is *a federal state*.

senses.gloss: Of the US national government, not the government of a state.
examples: Kidnapping is a *federal* crime.
He works for a *federal* agency in Washington.
*Federal* taxes are due in April.

senses.gloss: Of a country or system: made of states or regions that share power with a central government.
examples: The United States and Germany both have *federal* systems of government.
Canada is a *federal* country with ten provinces.

senses.gloss: Physically very weak.
examples: Her grandmother was too *feeble* to walk alone.
He spoke in a *feeble* voice.

senses.gloss: Not effective or convincing.
examples: That's a *feeble* excuse.
The team made a *feeble* attempt to come back.
That was the *feeblest* joke I've ever heard.

contrast: The g is silent: FAYND.

senses.gloss: Pretended; not real.
examples: She listened with *feigned* interest.
He looked up in *feigned* surprise.
Her *feigned* indifference didn't fool anyone.

senses.gloss: Full of energy and determination, and ready to argue or fight — often said with approval.
examples: My *feisty* 90-year-old grandma still argues with everyone.
The little dog is *feistier* than the big one.
She gave a *feisty* speech against the plan.

contrast: *A feline* is also a noun, meaning a cat.

senses.gloss: Relating to cats or the cat family.
examples: *Feline* diseases spread quickly in shelters.
Lions and tigers are *feline* predators.

senses.gloss: Like a cat, especially graceful, quiet or sly.
examples: She moved with *feline* grace.
His eyes had a *feline* look.

contrast: *Female* is about sex, used for animals, forms and statistics (*female workers*, *a female cat*); *feminine* describes qualities traditionally linked to women. As a noun, *a female* for a woman sounds clinical or rude, so say *a woman*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the sex that can have babies or lay eggs.
examples: Only *female* mosquitoes bite.
The company has only two *female* executives.
Is your kitten male or *female*?

senses.gloss: Of a plug or part: with a hole that another part fits into.
examples: You need a cable with a *female* connector on one end.
Screw the pipe into the *female* fitting.

senses.gloss: Having qualities traditionally thought typical of women.
examples: She likes soft, *feminine* colors like pink and lavender.
The dress is very *feminine*.
Her new haircut looks *more feminine*.

senses.gloss: In grammar: belonging to the gender class that includes most words for women.
examples: In Spanish, *casa* is a *feminine* noun.
Russian adjectives change their endings to agree with *feminine* nouns.

senses.gloss: Supporting equal rights and opportunities for women.
examples: She wrote several *feminist* books in the 1970s.
The movie has a strong *feminist* message.
Is the new version *more feminist* than the original?

senses.gloss: Of an animal: living wild after being tame, or born to such animals.
examples: The neighborhood has a lot of *feral* cats.
*Feral* hogs are destroying farms in Texas.

senses.gloss: Wild and fierce, like a wild animal.
examples: The crowd let out a *feral* roar.
After a week in the woods, the boys looked *feral*.

senses.gloss: Very fierce and violent.
examples: The guard dog looked *ferocious*.
Bears can be *ferocious* when they protect their cubs.

senses.gloss: Very strong or intense.
examples: The *ferocious* heat kept everyone inside.
The bill faced *ferocious* opposition in the Senate.
The competition is *more ferocious* than ever.

ru: плодородный; способный иметь детей; богатый (о воображении)
contrast: American English says FUR-tuhl; British English says FUR-tyl.

senses.gloss: Of land or soil: able to produce good crops.
examples: The valley has rich, *fertile* soil.
The Midwest has some of the *most fertile* farmland in the world.

senses.gloss: Of people or animals: able to have babies.
examples: Doctors ran tests to see if he was *fertile*.
Women are most *fertile* a few days each month.

senses.gloss: Of the mind or a situation: producing many ideas or good results.
examples: The writer has a *fertile* imagination.
The city was *fertile* ground for new bands.

senses.gloss: Having or showing very strong and sincere feelings about something.
examples: She's a *fervent* supporter of animal rights.
It is my *fervent* hope that they find a cure.
His fans are *more fervent* than ever.

contrast: *The festive season* is mostly British; Americans usually say *the holidays* or *the holiday season*.

senses.gloss: Cheerful and colorful in a way that suits a holiday or celebration.
examples: The streets looked *festive* with all the lights.
Everyone was in a *festive* mood.
Let's make the table a little *more festive*.

contrast: *The fetal position* is lying curled up on your side with your knees near your chest.

senses.gloss: Relating to a baby that is still developing inside its mother.
examples: The doctor checked the *fetal* heartbeat.
Drinking during pregnancy can harm *fetal* development.
He lay curled up in the *fetal* position.
